title: Inference Internals: KV Cache, Prefill/Decode, Batching, Speculation
scopeHtml: Scope: What happens inside an inference server: KV cache, the two phases, latency metrics, scheduling and draft-model speedups.

notes.title: The generation loop: why inference has internals at all
notes.html:
Start from zero. A large language model (LLM) is a function that reads a list of tokens (small pieces of text, roughly three quarters of a word in English) and returns a probability for every possible next token. To write a sentence, a server runs that function, picks one token (see the sampling notes for how), appends it to the list and runs the function again. This is called autoregressive generation: each new token depends on all the previous ones.

prompt tokens:  [The] [cat] [sat]
step 1: model reads [The][cat][sat]          -> picks [on]
step 2: model reads [The][cat][sat][on]      -> picks [the]
step 3: model reads [The][cat][sat][on][the] -> picks [mat]
step 4: ...                                  -> picks <end>

Two facts follow and drive everything in this note.

  1. One token per step, strictly in order. You cannot compute token 10 before token 9 exists. The loop cannot be parallelised across time for a single user.
  2. Each step looks at the whole history. Inside the model, the attention mechanism lets the newest token "look back" at every earlier token. Done naively, step 100 repeats the work of steps 1 to 99.

The naive cost is easy to count. If a prompt has P tokens and you generate N tokens without any reuse, step k reprocesses P + k tokens, so the total tokens pushed through the model is about N x P + N(N+1)/2. For P = 1,000 and N = 500 that is 500,000 + 125,250 = 625,250 token-passes, when only 1,500 distinct tokens exist. The first fix for this waste is the KV cache, and the second and third fixes (batching and speculation) attack the other big cost: the GPU sits mostly idle while generating one token.

Where does the product world meet this? When you call a hosted API such as Anthropic, OpenAI or Gemini, or run a model yourself with vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM, Hugging Face TGI or llama.cpp, everything below happens behind the HTTP endpoint. You rarely write this code, but you must reason about it: it explains why the first word is slow, why later words are fast, why long prompts cost more, why a busy server feels slower, and why a cheaper "cached input" price exists.

See also: C2 note 01_I1 covers the same topics at survey level (metrics table, PagedAttention, streaming, capacity planning). This note goes deeper on mechanism, byte-level math, runnable toy code, and failure modes.

Everyday analogy. Writing a letter one word at a time, where before each word you must re-read the entire letter from the top. A good writer would instead keep a running understanding in their head. That running understanding is the KV cache.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying the model "generates the whole answer at once". It produces one token per forward pass; streaming is just showing those passes as they finish.
  • Thinking output length is free. Every output token is another full pass through the model, so output tokens cost more than input tokens on almost every API (verify current pricing).
  • Confusing a token with a word or a character. Counts differ by tokenizer; never estimate cost from word counts alone.

notes.title: KV cache: what it is and why it exists
notes.html:
What attention needs. In each attention layer, every token is turned into three vectors: a query (Q, "what am I looking for"), a key (K, "what do I contain") and a value (V, "what information do I hand over if chosen"). The new token's query is compared against the keys of all earlier tokens to get weights, and the output is a weighted sum of their values.

The key insight: for an earlier token, its K and V vectors never change once computed (the model is causal, so a token never looks forward, and the weights are fixed at inference time). Recomputing them every step is pure waste. So the server stores them: the KV cache.

Without cache, step t:   compute Q,K,V for tokens 1..t   (t tokens of work)
With cache, step t:      compute Q,K,V for token t only  (1 token of work)
                         read K,V of tokens 1..t-1 from memory
                         attend: q_t . [K_1..K_t] -> weights -> sum of [V_1..V_t]
                         append K_t, V_t to the cache

Notice what the cache does NOT store: queries (only the newest token's query is needed, then discarded) and the final output probabilities. It stores K and V for every layer and every attention head, for every token seen so far.

What it buys. With the cache, the cost of generating N tokens after a P-token prompt drops from roughly N x P + N^2/2 token-passes to P + N (the prompt once, then one new token per step). In the earlier example: 1,500 token-passes instead of 625,250, about 400x less linear-layer work. The attention step still has to read all cached K and V each step (cost grows with length), but that is a memory read, not a recomputation of the projections and the feed-forward layers, which are the bulk of the compute.

The trade: memory for compute. You exchange recomputation for storage. That storage is large, grows with every token, and lives in the scarce GPU memory (HBM). Most of the rest of this note is a consequence of that trade.

Toy implementation (single head, numpy). This shows the mechanism: the cache is just two growing arrays, and each step adds one row.

import numpy as np

d = 4                                   # tiny head dimension
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
Wq, Wk, Wv = (rng.normal(size=(d, d)) for _ in range(3))

K_cache, V_cache = [], []               # the KV cache for one layer, one head

def step(x):                            # x: embedding of the NEWEST token only, shape (d,)
    q, k, v = x @ Wq, x @ Wk, x @ Wv
    K_cache.append(k); V_cache.append(v)        # append, never recompute old rows
    K, V = np.stack(K_cache), np.stack(V_cache) # shape (t, d)
    scores = K @ q / np.sqrt(d)                 # one score per cached token
    w = np.exp(scores - scores.max()); w /= w.sum()   # softmax
    return w @ V                                # weighted sum of values, shape (d,)

for t in range(3):
    out = step(rng.normal(size=d))
    print(t + 1, "cached tokens ->", out.round(2))   # prints 3 lines; cache length 1, 2, 3
import kotlin.math.exp
import kotlin.math.sqrt

const val D = 4
fun matVec(w: Array<DoubleArray>, x: DoubleArray) =
    DoubleArray(D) { j -> (0 until D).sumOf { i -> x[i] * w[i][j] } }

class HeadCache(val wq: Array<DoubleArray>, val wk: Array<DoubleArray>, val wv: Array<DoubleArray>) {
    private val keys = ArrayList<DoubleArray>()      // grows by one row per token
    private val values = ArrayList<DoubleArray>()

    fun step(x: DoubleArray): DoubleArray {
        val q = matVec(wq, x)
        keys += matVec(wk, x); values += matVec(wv, x)   // append only
        val scores = keys.map { k -> k.indices.sumOf { k[it] * q[it] } / sqrt(D.toDouble()) }
        val m = scores.max()
        val e = scores.map { exp(it - m) }; val s = e.sum()
        return DoubleArray(D) { j -> values.indices.sumOf { t -> e[t] / s * values[t][j] } }
    }
}
// Returns one output vector per call; keys.size grows 1, 2, 3 ...
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

public class HeadCache {
    static final int D = 4;
    final double[][] wq, wk, wv;
    final List<double[]> keys = new ArrayList<>(), values = new ArrayList<>();

    HeadCache(double[][] wq, double[][] wk, double[][] wv) { this.wq = wq; this.wk = wk; this.wv = wv; }

    static double[] matVec(double[][] w, double[] x) {
        double[] out = new double[D];
        for (int j = 0; j < D; j++) for (int i = 0; i < D; i++) out[j] += x[i] * w[i][j];
        return out;
    }

    double[] step(double[] x) {
        double[] q = matVec(wq, x);
        keys.add(matVec(wk, x)); values.add(matVec(wv, x));      // append only
        int t = keys.size();
        double[] e = new double[t]; double max = Double.NEGATIVE_INFINITY, sum = 0;
        double[] s = new double[t];
        for (int i = 0; i < t; i++) {
            for (int j = 0; j < D; j++) s[i] += keys.get(i)[j] * q[j];
            s[i] /= Math.sqrt(D); max = Math.max(max, s[i]);
        }
        for (int i = 0; i < t; i++) { e[i] = Math.exp(s[i] - max); sum += e[i]; }
        double[] out = new double[D];
        for (int i = 0; i < t; i++) for (int j = 0; j < D; j++) out[j] += e[i] / sum * values.get(i)[j];
        return out;                                              // keys.size() is 1, 2, 3 ...
    }
}

In a real model this happens in every layer (for example 32 or 80), for every KV head, on the GPU, with the cache laid out as large tensors, not Java lists. In Hugging Face Transformers the cache object is past_key_values (and use_cache=True is the default for generate); in vLLM the cache is managed by the block manager described later.

Real products. Every production LLM server uses it; it is not optional. Anthropic's, OpenAI's and Google's "prompt caching" features expose a related idea at the API level: they keep the KV cache of a stable prompt prefix so the next request can skip recomputing it (see the prefix caching section).

Everyday analogy. Reading a mystery novel and keeping a notebook of clues. On each new page you consult the notebook and add one line; you never reread chapters 1 to 10 from scratch.

Common interview traps.

  • "The KV cache stores the model's answers." No: it stores per-layer key and value tensors of tokens already processed, nothing about the output text.
  • "The cache makes attention free." Each step still reads the whole cache; cost per step grows with context length. The cache only removes recomputation.
  • "Queries are cached too." They are not; a past token's query is never needed again.

notes.title: KV cache memory math: why long context is expensive
notes.html:
You must be able to compute this on a whiteboard. The formula for bytes of cache per token is:

bytes_per_token = 2 (K and V) x layers x kv_heads x head_dim x bytes_per_value

Worked example 1: Llama-3-8B style (GQA). 32 layers, 8 KV heads, head dimension 128, fp16/bf16 (2 bytes per value). These are the published architecture numbers for Llama 3 8B (verify against the model card for any model you plan with).

2 x 32 x 8 x 128 x 2 = 131,072 bytes = 128 KiB per token
8,192-token context:   8,192 x 128 KiB = 1,048,576 KiB = 1 GiB per sequence

Worked example 2: Llama-2-7B style (full multi-head attention). 32 layers, 32 KV heads, head dimension 128, fp16.

2 x 32 x 32 x 128 x 2 = 524,288 bytes = 512 KiB per token
4,096-token context:   4,096 x 512 KiB = 2,097,152 KiB = 2 GiB per sequence

The difference between the two is grouped-query attention (GQA): several query heads share one K/V head, so 32 query heads need only 8 KV heads, a 4x smaller cache. Multi-query attention (MQA) goes to a single KV head. DeepSeek's multi-head latent attention (MLA) compresses K and V into a small latent vector. These are architecture choices made precisely to shrink the cache.

Why it matters: the capacity question. Say an 80 GB GPU holds an 8B model in bf16 (about 16 GB of weights; 8 billion x 2 bytes). Suppose you reserve 90 percent of memory and ~2 GB for activations: usable cache is roughly 80 x 0.9 - 16 - 2 = 54 GB (a rough planning number, not a measured one). At 1 GiB per 8k-token sequence, that is about 54 simultaneous full-length sequences. At 128k context (16 GiB per sequence at the same 128 KiB/token) it is only about 3. So the batch size is limited by cache memory, not by compute, and that decides throughput and cost per token.

Tiny calculator in three languages.

def kv_bytes(layers, kv_heads, head_dim, tokens, dtype_bytes=2):
    return 2 * layers * kv_heads * head_dim * dtype_bytes * tokens

gib = kv_bytes(32, 8, 128, 8192) / 2**30
print(f"{gib:.2f} GiB")          # prints 1.00 GiB
fun kvBytes(layers: Int, kvHeads: Int, headDim: Int, tokens: Long, dtypeBytes: Int = 2): Long =
    2L * layers * kvHeads * headDim * dtypeBytes * tokens

fun main() {
    val gib = kvBytes(32, 8, 128, 8192) / Math.pow(2.0, 30.0)
    println("%.2f GiB".format(gib))   // prints 1.00 GiB
}
public class KvMath {
    static long kvBytes(int layers, int kvHeads, int headDim, long tokens, int dtypeBytes) {
        return 2L * layers * kvHeads * headDim * dtypeBytes * tokens;
    }
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        double gib = kvBytes(32, 8, 128, 8192, 2) / Math.pow(2, 30);
        System.out.printf("%.2f GiB%n", gib);   // prints 1.00 GiB
    }
}

Levers to shrink it. (1) GQA/MQA/MLA architectures. (2) KV-cache quantization: store values in fp8 or int8 instead of fp16, halving memory (vLLM exposes a KV cache dtype option; quality impact must be tested, verify the flag in current docs). (3) Sliding-window attention, used by some models in some layers, which caps how many past tokens a layer keeps. (4) Truncating or summarising context at the application level. (5) Offloading cold cache to CPU RAM or disk at the price of transfer latency.

Android angle. On-device LLMs (Gemini Nano, MediaPipe LLM Inference with a Gemma model) hit the same wall in tiny form: phone RAM is shared with the OS and apps, so the context length limit is mostly a KV cache budget. That is why on-device runtimes expose a maximum token setting.

Everyday analogy. A hotel where every guest (sequence) keeps adding luggage (cache) for the length of their stay. The number of guests the hotel can host is set by luggage storage, not by the number of staff.

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting the factor 2 (keys AND values) or using attention heads instead of KV heads for GQA models.
  • Believing model weights dominate memory at scale. For many concurrent long requests the KV cache exceeds the weights.
  • Quoting memory per request as fixed: it grows linearly with context length and the cache lives until the request ends (or is evicted).

notes.title: Prefill versus decode: two very different phases
notes.html:
Every request has two phases that stress the hardware in opposite ways.

Prefill (prompt processing). All P prompt tokens are known up front, so the model processes them in one big parallel pass, building the KV cache for each layer and producing the logits (scores) for the first output token. Matrix multiplications are huge ([P tokens] x [weights]), so the GPU's arithmetic units are the bottleneck: compute-bound.

Decode (generation). Each step processes exactly one new token per sequence. To do that, the GPU must still stream all model weights from memory (say 16 GB) plus the sequence's cache, to do a tiny amount of math. The bottleneck is memory bandwidth: memory-bound.

            PREFILL                         DECODE
tokens in   P (e.g. 2,000) at once          1 per sequence per step
GPU limit   compute (FLOPs)                 memory bandwidth (GB/s)
output      KV cache + 1st token            1 token per step
time        one burst, ~ proportional P     N steps, each ~ constant
user feels  "TTFT" wait                     streaming speed

Numbers (show the math). Take an 8B model in bf16 on a GPU with about 2 TB/s memory bandwidth and about 1,000 TFLOPs of usable bf16 compute (round, illustrative numbers; real parts differ, verify your hardware spec).

  • Decode, batch 1: one step reads ~16 GB. Time >= 16 GB / 2,000 GB/s = 8 ms. Maths done: about 2 FLOPs x 8 x 10^9 params = 16 GFLOPs, which the GPU could finish in 16 x 10^9 / 10^15 = 0.016 ms. So the compute units are busy about 0.2 percent of the step. Max about 125 tokens/s.
  • Prefill, 2,000-token prompt: FLOPs about 2 x 8 x 10^9 x 2,000 = 3.2 x 10^13 = 32 TFLOPs. At 10^15 FLOPs/s that is about 32 ms of pure compute, plus the same 8 ms weight read overlapped. So prefill of 2,000 tokens takes tens of milliseconds, in practice more because real utilisation is well below peak.

The ratio of arithmetic to bytes moved is the arithmetic intensity. Decode at batch 1 has about 1 FLOP per byte; a modern GPU needs hundreds to saturate compute. That gap is the room that batching and speculation exploit.

The quadratic part. Prefill attention compares every prompt token with every earlier one, which grows with P squared, while the dense layers grow linearly with P. For short prompts the linear part dominates; for very long prompts (tens of thousands of tokens) attention takes over, which is why long-context prefill is slow and why FlashAttention (a kernel that avoids writing the big attention matrix to memory) matters.

Observing the phases. Ask for max_tokens=1 to measure roughly prefill time. Ask for a short prompt and max_tokens=500 to measure decode speed. Real servers publish these separately (vLLM exposes time-to-first-token and inter-token-latency histograms on its Prometheus metrics endpoint; check the metric names in the docs for your version).

Interference. When a new long prompt arrives, its compute-heavy prefill occupies the GPU, and running users' decode steps are delayed, producing visible stalls in streaming. Fixes: chunked prefill (split the prompt into chunks of, say, 512 to 2,048 tokens and mix one chunk with the decode tokens of others each step), and disaggregated serving, which runs prefill on one set of GPUs and decode on another and ships the KV cache between them (research systems such as DistServe and Splitwise, and production support emerging in vLLM and others; verify current status).

Prompt caching connects here. If the first 90 percent of a prompt is identical to a previous request, the server can reuse that cached KV state and only prefill the new 10 percent. That cuts prefill compute and TTFT, which is why hosted APIs charge less for cached input tokens and why you should put stable content (system prompt, tool definitions, reference documents) first and variable content last.

Everyday analogy. A chef reading the whole order slip and prepping ingredients (prefill: lots of thinking in one go), then plating dishes one at a time while the oven, not the chef's brain, is the limit (decode).

Common interview traps.

  • Saying decode is slow because of "heavy computation". It is slow because of reading weights from memory; compute is mostly idle.
  • Assuming input and output tokens cost the same time. Input tokens are processed in parallel; output tokens are one-by-one, which is why output is priced higher.
  • Claiming a longer prompt only affects TTFT. It also enlarges the cache read at every decode step and consumes cache memory, hurting batch size.

notes.title: TTFT, tokens per second and the other latency numbers
notes.html:
Users feel a streaming chat as two things: how long before anything appears, and how fast text flows afterward. Engineers add system-level numbers.

Metric Plain meaning Formula or note
TTFT Time to first token: request sent until first token arrives queue wait + prefill + network
TPOT or ITL Time per output token / inter-token latency (end - first token) / (output tokens - 1)
Per-user tokens/s Streaming speed one user sees 1 / TPOT
E2E latency Total request time TTFT + TPOT x (N - 1)
System throughput Tokens/s across all users sum over concurrent requests
Goodput Throughput of requests that met their latency target what you actually sell

Worked example. TTFT 400 ms, TPOT 25 ms, 300 output tokens. E2E = 0.4 s + 0.025 x 299 = 0.4 + 7.475 = 7.875 s. Per-user speed = 1 / 0.025 = 40 tokens/s, faster than comfortable reading speed (about 5 to 10 tokens/s), so a human would not notice 25 ms but would notice a 400 ms start. Now double the prompt length: if prefill dominates TTFT and scales roughly linearly, TTFT goes to about 700 ms (assuming 100 ms of fixed overhead and 300 ms of prefill doubling to 600), E2E barely changes. For a 20-token answer, though, TTFT dominates E2E.

Latency versus throughput. The two metrics trade off. Bigger batches raise system tokens/s (and lower cost per token) but each step takes longer and requests may wait longer in the queue, so per-user speed and TTFT worsen. You choose a target (a service-level objective, SLO) such as "p95 TTFT under 1 s and p95 TPOT under 50 ms" and then maximise throughput while staying inside it. That constrained throughput is goodput.

Always use percentiles. The mean hides the pain. p50 is the median, p95 and p99 are the slow tail. A few very long prompts or a burst of arrivals push p99 TTFT up while the mean looks fine.

Measuring against any OpenAI-compatible server (vLLM, SGLang, Ollama, and many hosted APIs). Stream the response and time the first chunk and the chunk count.

import time
from openai import OpenAI   # pip install openai; works against vLLM/Ollama via base_url

client = OpenAI(base_url="http://localhost:8000/v1", api_key="EMPTY")  # local server; key from env for hosted
t0 = time.perf_counter()
first = None
chunks = 0
stream = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct",   # whatever your server loaded
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Explain the KV cache in 200 words."}],
    stream=True, max_tokens=300)
for ev in stream:
    if ev.choices and ev.choices[0].delta.content:
        chunks += 1
        if first is None:
            first = time.perf_counter()
end = time.perf_counter()
ttft = first - t0
tpot = (end - first) / max(chunks - 1, 1)     # a chunk is usually one token, but not guaranteed
print(f"TTFT {ttft*1000:.0f} ms, TPOT {tpot*1000:.1f} ms, {1/tpot:.0f} tok/s")  # prints three measured numbers
import java.net.URI
import java.net.http.HttpClient
import java.net.http.HttpRequest
import java.net.http.HttpResponse

fun main() {
    val body = """{"model":"meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct","stream":true,"max_tokens":300,
        "messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Explain the KV cache in 200 words."}]}"""
    val req = HttpRequest.newBuilder(URI("http://localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions"))
        .header("Content-Type", "application/json")
        .POST(HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.ofString(body)).build()
    val t0 = System.nanoTime(); var first = 0L; var chunks = 0
    HttpClient.newHttpClient().send(req, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofLines()).body().use { lines ->
        lines.forEach { line ->                       // server-sent events: "data: {json}"
            if (line.startsWith("data:") && !line.contains("[DONE]")) {
                if (first == 0L) first = System.nanoTime()
                chunks++
            }
        }
    }
    val end = System.nanoTime()
    println("TTFT ${(first - t0) / 1e6} ms, TPOT ${(end - first) / 1e6 / maxOf(chunks - 1, 1)} ms")
}
// Prints two measured numbers. Android: run this on your backend, not on the phone UI thread.
import java.net.URI;
import java.net.http.*;

public class Ttft {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        String body = "{\"model\":\"meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct\",\"stream\":true,\"max_tokens\":300,"
            + "\"messages\":[{\"role\":\"user\",\"content\":\"Explain the KV cache in 200 words.\"}]}";
        HttpRequest req = HttpRequest.newBuilder(URI.create("http://localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions"))
            .header("Content-Type", "application/json")
            .POST(HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.ofString(body)).build();
        long t0 = System.nanoTime(), first = 0; int chunks = 0;
        try (var lines = HttpClient.newHttpClient().send(req, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofLines()).body()) {
            for (var it = lines.iterator(); it.hasNext();) {
                String line = it.next();
                if (line.startsWith("data:") && !line.contains("[DONE]")) {
                    if (first == 0) first = System.nanoTime();
                    chunks++;
                }
            }
        }
        long end = System.nanoTime();
        System.out.printf("TTFT %.0f ms, TPOT %.1f ms%n", (first - t0) / 1e6, (end - first) / 1e6 / Math.max(chunks - 1, 1));
    }
}

Real benchmarking tools: vLLM ships benchmark scripts, NVIDIA GenAI-Perf, and open-source load generators such as GuideLLM; check current names in docs. For fair numbers, replay a realistic mix of prompt and output lengths at a controlled request rate.

Tail-latency causes. Queueing under bursts; a long prefill blocking decode; cache memory exhaustion causing preemption (the scheduler pauses a request, drops its cache, and recomputes later); cold starts of GPU nodes; noisy network or a gateway buffering the stream (buffering in a reverse proxy makes streaming look like one big delayed response; disable response buffering for SSE).

Everyday analogy. A coffee shop: TTFT is how long until your first sip, TPOT is how quickly refills arrive after that, and throughput is cups per hour for the whole queue. Hiring a bigger batch of customers per barista raises cups per hour but makes each person wait longer.

Common interview traps.

  • Reporting only average latency or only tokens/s. Interviewers want TTFT and TPOT separately plus p95/p99.
  • Using system throughput as proof that one user is fast. Total 4,000 tokens/s across 32 users is about 125 tokens/s each at best.
  • Counting SSE chunks as tokens blindly. Chunks may batch several tokens, or the first chunk may be a role header; use the server's usage statistics when exact counts matter.

notes.title: Continuous batching: scheduling at every step
notes.html:
Why batch at all. In decode, loading the weights dominates the step time (8 ms for 16 GB at 2 TB/s in our example). Those weights serve one sequence or thirty-two equally; the extra math is nearly free until the GPU's compute or the cache memory is exhausted. Batch 32 at roughly 8 ms per step yields 32 tokens per 8 ms = 4,000 tokens/s versus 125 tokens/s at batch 1. Each user still sees about the same speed, but cost per token drops by roughly 30x. (Real steps get slower as batch and cache reads grow, so treat 30x as an upper bound.)

Static batching (the old way). Collect N requests, run them together until every one has finished. Problems:

  1. The batch lasts as long as its longest answer. A 20-token answer next to a 500-token answer holds a GPU slot idle for 480 steps.
  2. New arrivals wait for the whole batch to end (high TTFT).
  3. Inputs must be padded to equal length, wasting compute.

Continuous batching (also called in-flight or iteration-level batching). Introduced in the Orca paper (OSDI 2022) and adopted by vLLM, TGI, TensorRT-LLM and SGLang. The scheduler runs at every decode step, not once per batch:

step 1: [A][B][C][D]     all running
step 2: [A][B][C][D]
step 3: [A][B][C][D]     C emits <end> -> C leaves
step 4: [A][B][E][D]     E (waiting in queue) joins immediately
step 5: [A][B][E][D]     ...

A finished sequence frees its slot and its cache blocks instantly; a queued request enters at the next iteration (its prefill is run, ideally chunked, alongside others' decode tokens). The GPU stays full and short requests are not held hostage by long ones. Reported throughput gains over static batching are several-fold on mixed workloads (the vLLM and Orca papers report large factors; exact numbers depend on workload, so verify rather than memorise).

Scheduler rules in a real server (vLLM-style).

  • max_num_seqs: maximum sequences running concurrently.
  • max_num_batched_tokens: token budget per step (decode tokens plus prefill chunk tokens). A smaller budget protects decode latency; a larger one favours throughput and TTFT of new prompts.
  • Free KV blocks gate admission: a request enters only if its prompt fits and there is room to grow. If memory runs out mid-flight, the scheduler preempts a request (swap its blocks out or recompute later).
  • Policy: first-come-first-served by default; priority scheduling exists in some servers. (Option names are from vLLM; verify exact spellings for your version.)

Toy scheduler. This simulates the idea with fake "work": each request needs a number of output steps; each loop iteration is one decode step of the whole batch.

from collections import deque

def run(requests, max_batch=3):             # requests: list of (name, steps_needed)
    waiting, running, step, done_at = deque(requests), {}, 0, {}
    while waiting or running:
        while waiting and len(running) < max_batch:     # admit at EVERY step
            name, n = waiting.popleft(); running[name] = n
        step += 1
        for name in list(running):                      # one decode step for everyone
            running[name] -= 1
            if running[name] == 0:
                del running[name]; done_at[name] = step # slot freed immediately
    return done_at

print(run([("A", 2), ("B", 8), ("C", 2), ("D", 2), ("E", 2)]))
# prints {'A': 2, 'C': 2, 'D': 4, 'E': 4, 'B': 8}
fun run(requests: List<Pair<String, Int>>, maxBatch: Int = 3): Map<String, Int> {
    val waiting = ArrayDeque(requests)
    val running = LinkedHashMap<String, Int>()
    val doneAt = LinkedHashMap<String, Int>()
    var step = 0
    while (waiting.isNotEmpty() || running.isNotEmpty()) {
        while (waiting.isNotEmpty() && running.size < maxBatch) {   // admit at every step
            val (name, n) = waiting.removeFirst(); running[name] = n
        }
        step++
        for (name in running.keys.toList()) {                      // one decode step for all
            running[name] = running.getValue(name) - 1
            if (running[name] == 0) { running.remove(name); doneAt[name] = step }
        }
    }
    return doneAt
}

fun main() = println(run(listOf("A" to 2, "B" to 8, "C" to 2, "D" to 2, "E" to 2)))
// prints {A=2, C=2, D=4, E=4, B=8}
import java.util.*;

public class ContinuousBatching {
    static Map<String, Integer> run(List<Map.Entry<String, Integer>> reqs, int maxBatch) {
        Deque<Map.Entry<String, Integer>> waiting = new ArrayDeque<>(reqs);
        Map<String, Integer> running = new LinkedHashMap<>(), doneAt = new LinkedHashMap<>();
        int step = 0;
        while (!waiting.isEmpty() || !running.isEmpty()) {
            while (!waiting.isEmpty() && running.size() < maxBatch) {      // admit at every step
                var r = waiting.poll(); running.put(r.getKey(), r.getValue());
            }
            step++;
            for (String name : new ArrayList<>(running.keySet())) {        // one decode step for all
                int left = running.get(name) - 1;
                if (left == 0) { running.remove(name); doneAt.put(name, step); }
                else running.put(name, left);
            }
        }
        return doneAt;
    }
    public static void main(String[] a) {
        System.out.println(run(List.of(Map.entry("A", 2), Map.entry("B", 8), Map.entry("C", 2),
            Map.entry("D", 2), Map.entry("E", 2)), 3));   // prints {A=2, C=2, D=4, E=4, B=8}
    }
}

Check by hand: with a batch of 3, A, B, C start; A and C finish at step 2, so D and E enter at step 3 and finish at step 4, while B runs to step 8. A static batcher would run {A,B,C} for 8 steps, then {D,E} for 2 more steps, so D and E would finish at step 10 instead of 4.

Production failure patterns.

  • Head-of-line blocking from long prompts without chunked prefill: a 50k-token prompt freezes everyone's streaming for seconds.
  • Over-admission: batch limit set too high; cache fills, the server preempts and recomputes repeatedly (thrashing), throughput collapses while GPU shows high utilisation. Watch preemption counters and cache usage metrics.
  • Fairness: one tenant floods the queue. Add per-tenant rate limits and priority classes at the gateway.
  • Backpressure: when queue length rises, return HTTP 429 or 503 early rather than letting TTFT grow without bound.

Everyday analogy. A bus that lets passengers off and on at every stop, instead of a train that waits at the station until the last passenger of the previous trip has reached the final destination.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying continuous batching "makes each request faster". It raises system throughput and lowers waiting time for new requests; a single request's token speed is about the same or slightly slower.
  • Mixing up it with "dynamic batching" (wait a few ms to group requests), which is the older, request-level technique used for classifiers.
  • Forgetting that batch size is bounded by KV cache memory as much as by compute.

notes.title: Prefix caching and paged cache memory
notes.html:
Continuous batching only works if cache memory can be given and taken back cheaply at every step. This is where PagedAttention (vLLM, 2023) comes in; see also note 01_I1 for the summary. Here is the mechanism step by step.

The old problem. Early servers reserved one contiguous region per request sized for the maximum possible length (say 2,048 tokens), because the final length is unknown. A request that stops at 200 tokens wastes 90 percent of its region (internal fragmentation), and free gaps between regions are too small to reuse (external fragmentation). The vLLM paper measured that existing systems wasted roughly 60 to 80 percent of KV memory this way (verify the exact figures in the paper).

The fix. Split the cache into fixed blocks of, say, 16 tokens. A request owns a block table, a list mapping its logical blocks (0, 1, 2, ...) to physical blocks anywhere in GPU memory, allocated on demand as it generates.

request A logical blocks:  [0] [1] [2]            block table A: 7, 1, 12
request B logical blocks:  [0] [1]                block table B: 3, 9
physical memory:  | 0 | 1:A1 | 2 | 3:B0 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7:A0 | 8 | 9:B1 | 10 | 11 | 12:A2 |

Block size arithmetic: with 128 KiB per token (Llama-3-8B example above) and 16-token blocks, one block is 16 x 128 KiB = 2 MiB. Waste per sequence is at most one partially filled block (under 16 tokens, under 2 MiB), which is tiny compared to reserving the maximum length.

Prefix caching (sharing). If two requests begin with the same tokens, their first blocks hold identical K/V values. The server can compute a hash of each full block (including its preceding tokens), look it up in a table, and point the new request's block table at the existing physical blocks, skipping that part of prefill entirely. Blocks are reference-counted; writes use copy-on-write when sequences diverge. vLLM calls this automatic prefix caching; SGLang's RadixAttention stores prefixes in a radix tree for the same purpose.

Practical consequences:

  • A fixed 3,000-token system prompt shared by every request is prefilled once, then reused: TTFT drops sharply and prefill compute is saved.
  • The match must be an exact token prefix. Putting a timestamp or user name at the top of the prompt breaks sharing for everything after it. Put changing content last.
  • Cached blocks occupy memory until evicted (typically least-recently-used). Cache hit rate is a metric worth tracking.

Hosted APIs expose the same idea as prompt caching (Anthropic uses explicit cache breakpoints with a time-to-live; OpenAI applies it automatically to long repeated prefixes; Gemini supports implicit and explicit caching). Minimum cacheable length, discounts and TTLs change; verify on the current pricing pages.

Failure patterns. Hit rate collapsing after a prompt template change (a single character moved earlier in the prompt); multi-tenant isolation worries (hashes must be scoped so one tenant cannot infer another's prompts by timing; some providers isolate caches per organisation); cache memory competing with active sequences so heavy prefix retention reduces batch size.

Everyday analogy. A library that shelves books anywhere there is space and keeps an index card listing which shelf slots hold your book, so no one needs a whole empty aisle reserved. Two readers of the same chapter are pointed at the same copy.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing prefix caching works for any similar text. Only an identical token prefix hits; "mostly the same" does not.
  • Thinking prefix caching changes outputs. It must not: it is the same K/V values, only reused (small numeric differences from different batch shapes can exist, see determinism notes).
  • Ignoring that cache hits depend on routing: with several replicas, requests sharing a prefix should reach the same replica (cache-aware routing) or the hit rate divides by the replica count.

notes.title: Speculative decoding: faster generation with a draft model
notes.html:
Idea in plain words. Decode is memory-bound: checking 5 tokens at once costs almost the same as generating 1, because the weights are read once either way. So let a small, fast draft model guess the next few tokens, then let the big target model check all guesses in a single pass. Keep the guesses that the target agrees with, and take the target's own token at the first disagreement. When the draft is right often, you get several tokens for roughly the price of one big step.

Step by step (greedy case). Draft length gamma = 4.

context: "The capital of France is"
1. Draft model (tiny, fast) proposes: " Paris" "," " a" " city"       (4 cheap steps)
2. Target model runs ONE forward pass over context + 4 proposals,
   producing its own next-token choice at each of the 5 positions:
      after "is"          -> " Paris"   matches proposal 1  accept
      after "Paris"       -> ","        matches proposal 2  accept
      after ","           -> " the"     proposal 3 was " a"  REJECT, use " the"
3. Output this round: " Paris" "," " the"   (3 tokens from 1 big pass)
4. Next round starts from "... France is Paris, the"

Even the worst case yields at least one correct token per round (the target's own), so output never falls below the speed of plain decoding apart from the wasted draft cost.

Correctness for sampling. With sampling (temperature above 0), the accept rule is rejection sampling: accept the draft token x with probability min(1, p_target(x) / q_draft(x)); on rejection, sample from the normalised residual distribution max(0, p_target - q_draft). The papers (Leviathan et al. 2023, "Fast Inference from Transformers via Speculative Decoding"; Chen et al. 2023, DeepMind) prove the output distribution equals the target's exactly. So this is a lossless speed-up, unlike quantization or distillation.

Expected speed-up math. Let alpha be the probability that one draft token is accepted (assumed independent per token), and gamma the number of proposals. Expected tokens produced per target pass is:

E[tokens] = (1 - alpha^(gamma+1)) / (1 - alpha)

alpha = 0.8, gamma = 4:  alpha^5 = 0.8^5 = 0.32768
   E = (1 - 0.32768) / 0.2 = 0.67232 / 0.2 = 3.36 tokens per target pass
alpha = 0.5, gamma = 4:  0.5^5 = 0.03125
   E = (1 - 0.03125) / 0.5 = 1.9375 tokens per target pass

Now include the draft cost. Let c be the cost of one draft step relative to one target step. A round costs 1 + gamma x c target-step-equivalents. If c = 0.05 (a draft model 20x cheaper per step): round cost = 1 + 4 x 0.05 = 1.2. Speed-up at alpha 0.8 = 3.36 / 1.2 = 2.8x. At alpha 0.5 = 1.9375 / 1.2 = 1.6x. If c = 0.3 (a draft that is too big): cost = 1 + 4 x 0.3 = 2.2, speed-up at alpha 0.5 = 1.9375 / 2.2 = 0.88x, i.e. SLOWER than not speculating. This is the central trade-off: the draft must be both cheap and well aligned with the target.

What affects the acceptance rate. Draft and target should share the same tokenizer and ideally the same family and training data (a small Llama draft for a large Llama target). Predictable text (code, JSON, quoting from the prompt, boilerplate) has high acceptance; open-ended creative text and high temperature lower it.

Variants you should recognise.

  • Separate draft model: easiest to explain, costs extra GPU memory and its own KV cache.
  • Medusa: extra prediction heads attached to the target model, no second model; EAGLE (and EAGLE-2/3): a lightweight draft head operating on the target's hidden states, usually higher acceptance. Both usually need a trained head for your target model.
  • Prompt lookup / n-gram speculation: propose tokens by copying matching spans from the prompt. Needs no model at all and is excellent for summarisation, code editing and RAG answers that quote context. vLLM supports an n-gram option.
  • Tree-based verification: verify several candidate continuations in one pass using a tree attention mask.
  • Multi-token prediction (MTP): models such as DeepSeek-V3 are trained with extra prediction modules that can be used for speculation (verify details in the paper). Server support names change quickly (vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM, llama.cpp all have speculative options); verify flags in current docs.

When it hurts. With large batches the GPU is no longer memory-bound; verification of extra tokens becomes real compute and throughput can drop. Speculation is mainly a latency tool for low-to-medium load, and many deployments enable it for interactive traffic only. It also uses extra memory (draft weights and draft cache).

Toy greedy simulation. The "models" here are simple functions over integers so you can see accept/reject logic. Target continues the sequence n -> n+1 always; the draft is right except when n is a multiple of 4.

def target_next(n): return n + 1
def draft_next(n):  return n + 2 if n % 4 == 0 else n + 1   # wrong when n % 4 == 0

def speculate(last, gamma=4, rounds=3):
    out = []
    for _ in range(rounds):
        props, cur = [], last
        for _ in range(gamma):                   # draft proposes gamma tokens
            cur = draft_next(cur); props.append(cur)
        cur, accepted = last, []
        for p in props:                          # target verifies (one parallel pass in reality)
            t = target_next(cur)
            accepted.append(t)                   # target's own token is always correct
            if t != p: break                     # stop at first mismatch
            cur = p
        out += accepted; last = accepted[-1]
    return out

print(speculate(0))   # prints [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9]  (same as plain decoding)
fun targetNext(n: Int) = n + 1
fun draftNext(n: Int) = if (n % 4 == 0) n + 2 else n + 1

fun speculate(start: Int, gamma: Int = 4, rounds: Int = 3): List<Int> {
    val out = mutableListOf<Int>(); var last = start
    repeat(rounds) {
        val props = mutableListOf<Int>(); var cur = last
        repeat(gamma) { cur = draftNext(cur); props += cur }
        cur = last; val accepted = mutableListOf<Int>()
        for (p in props) {
            val t = targetNext(cur); accepted += t
            if (t != p) break                    // first mismatch: keep target's token, stop
            cur = p
        }
        out += accepted; last = accepted.last()
    }
    return out
}

fun main() = println(speculate(0))   // prints [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9]
import java.util.*;

public class Speculate {
    static int target(int n) { return n + 1; }
    static int draft(int n) { return n % 4 == 0 ? n + 2 : n + 1; }

    static List<Integer> speculate(int start, int gamma, int rounds) {
        List<Integer> out = new ArrayList<>(); int last = start;
        for (int r = 0; r < rounds; r++) {
            List<Integer> props = new ArrayList<>(); int cur = last;
            for (int i = 0; i < gamma; i++) { cur = draft(cur); props.add(cur); }
            cur = last; List<Integer> accepted = new ArrayList<>();
            for (int p : props) {
                int t = target(cur); accepted.add(t);
                if (t != p) break;               // first mismatch: keep target's token, stop
                cur = p;
            }
            out.addAll(accepted); last = accepted.get(accepted.size() - 1);
        }
        return out;
    }
    public static void main(String[] a) { System.out.println(speculate(0, 4, 3)); }
    // prints [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9]
}

The printed sequence is identical to what the target alone would produce (1 to 9), which is the lossless property. The gain is fewer expensive target passes: round 1 yields 1 token (the draft wrongly proposes 2 after 0), round 2 yields 4 (draft right three times, wrong at 6), round 3 yields 4 again, so 9 tokens cost 3 target passes instead of 9.

Products. Google uses speculative decoding in serving (reported for AI Overviews and Gemini; verify), vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM and Hugging Face Transformers (assisted generation) implement it, and llama.cpp supports a draft model option. Apple's on-device and various "fast mode" offerings from API providers use variants of it (specific claims vary, verify).

Everyday analogy. A junior writes a draft paragraph and a senior reads it in one go, striking out only the first wrong sentence and everything after it. Reading is faster than writing, so the team finishes sooner as long as the junior is usually right.

Common interview traps.

  • "Speculative decoding is approximate." In the standard algorithm the output distribution is exactly the target's; that is the point.
  • Picking the biggest draft model for best acceptance. Draft cost c erodes the gain, as the c = 0.3 example shows.
  • Claiming it always helps. It helps most when memory-bound (small batch, interactive); at high batch it can reduce throughput.
  • Forgetting the draft and target must share a tokenizer, or the token ids cannot be compared.

notes.title: Putting it together: the life of one request
notes.html:
Combine all pieces to follow one request through a vLLM-style server.

client ->  HTTP gateway (auth, rate limit, tenant quota)
       ->  router (cache-aware: same prefix -> same replica)
       ->  server queue
       ->  scheduler (every step):
             - admits request if free KV blocks and token budget allow
             - looks up prefix cache: skip already-cached prompt blocks
             - PREFILL (chunked) on remaining prompt tokens -> first token  (TTFT ends)
             - DECODE steps, batched with other requests, one token each
                 (optionally: draft proposes, target verifies several tokens)
             - on <end> or max_tokens: free blocks, leave batch
       ->  tokens streamed back via SSE

Timeline example with numbers. Prompt 2,000 tokens, of which 1,500 are a cached system prompt. Output 200 tokens. Assume prefill speed about 20,000 tokens/s for the model (illustrative), queue wait 50 ms, decode 25 ms per token under load.

  • Without prefix cache: prefill = 2,000 / 20,000 = 0.100 s. TTFT = 0.050 + 0.100 = 0.150 s (plus network).
  • With prefix cache: prefill only 500 tokens = 0.025 s. TTFT = 0.050 + 0.025 = 0.075 s, half as much.
  • Decode: 199 further tokens x 0.025 = 4.975 s. E2E = 0.075 + 4.975 = 5.05 s.
  • With speculation giving 2x fewer effective steps in decode (optimistic): about 2.5 s decode, E2E near 2.6 s.

Notice where each technique acts: prefix caching shortens the first part (TTFT), speculation shortens the second part (decode), continuous batching raises the whole system's tokens per dollar, and the KV cache underlies all three.

Configuring a local server (for hands-on learning). With vLLM you can start an OpenAI-compatible server with a command such as vllm serve <model> and options for max context length, GPU memory utilisation fraction, max sequences and prefix caching; llama.cpp's llama-server and Ollama give the same style of endpoint on a laptop. Option names and defaults change between versions: verify with --help for your version.

Backend integration, not phone integration. An Android app should never talk to a GPU server with embedded keys. Put your own backend (Spring Boot, Ktor, FastAPI) in the middle, which authenticates users, applies quotas and relays the stream as SSE or WebSocket. On-device models (Gemini Nano, MediaPipe LLM Inference) run their own tiny version of this loop with the same prefill and decode behaviour and a small KV cache budget.

Everyday analogy. A restaurant with a host (gateway), a kitchen scheduler (batcher), a prep station that remembers a standard sauce (prefix cache), and a sous chef who pre-chops while the head chef finishes dishes (speculation).

Common interview traps.

  • Describing each optimisation in isolation. Interviewers like candidates who say which phase and which metric each technique improves.
  • Forgetting the network and gateway: TTFT includes TLS, proxies and queueing, not only GPU time.
  • Optimising the model server while a proxy buffers the stream, so users still see nothing until the end.

notes.title: Production failure patterns and what to monitor
notes.html:
Symptoms and likely causes.

Symptom Likely cause First check
TTFT spikes, TPOT fine queueing or large prefills; prefix cache hit rate dropped queue length, prompt length distribution, cache hit rate
TPOT jitter, streaming stalls long prefills interleaving with decode; no chunked prefill chunked prefill setting, token budget per step
Throughput collapses at high load, GPU "busy" KV cache exhausted, preemption and recompute thrashing cache usage %, preemption counter
Out-of-memory at start or under load context length times concurrency exceeds cache; memory fraction too high max model length, max sequences, memory utilisation
Speculation made it slower low acceptance rate or high batch acceptance rate metric, batch size
Cost jumped with no traffic change prompt template changed and broke prefix/prompt caching cached-token ratio in usage stats
Identical prompts give different outputs batch-dependent numerics, non-greedy sampling see determinism notes

Metrics to export (names differ by server). Running and waiting requests; KV cache usage fraction; prefix cache hit rate; TTFT, TPOT and E2E histograms; tokens in and out per second; preemptions; for speculation, the accepted-token rate. Alert on p95 and p99, not on means.

Capacity rules of thumb. (1) Size by KV cache first: sequences you can hold = free cache memory / (bytes per token x average total tokens). (2) Test with your real prompt and output length distribution; average length hides the tail that fills memory. (3) Reserve headroom (for example run at 60 to 70 percent of the knee of the throughput curve) so bursts do not turn into tail-latency cliffs. (4) Separate traffic classes: interactive chat gets a tight latency SLO, batch jobs use spare capacity.

Protecting the service. Cap max_tokens and input length per tenant, enforce timeouts, cancel generation when the client disconnects (otherwise the GPU keeps decoding for nobody; make sure your gateway propagates cancellation), and shed load with 429/503 plus Retry-After rather than letting queues grow.

Everyday analogy. Running a highway: the metrics are traffic sensors, preemption is a closed lane causing a jam that outlasts the accident, and cancelling abandoned requests is clearing broken-down cars.

Common interview traps.

  • Treating GPU utilisation percentage as the health metric. A thrashing server can show 100 percent utilisation while useful throughput is low.
  • Forgetting client cancellation, which wastes real GPU time on responses nobody reads.
  • Load testing with identical short prompts, which hides cache exhaustion and tail behaviour.

notes.title: Choosing and explaining the techniques in an interview
notes.html:
A compact way to answer "how would you make LLM inference faster or cheaper?":

  1. First measure: split TTFT from TPOT, check p95, and find whether you are compute-bound (long prompts), memory-bandwidth-bound (decode) or cache-capacity-bound (many long sequences).
  2. Reduce work: shorten and reorder prompts (stable prefix first), cap output length, use prefix or prompt caching.
  3. Raise utilisation: continuous batching, chunked prefill, tuned token budget.
  4. Shrink memory: GQA models, KV cache quantization, weight quantization (see 02_Q1), shorter contexts.
  5. Cut decode steps: speculative decoding for latency-sensitive, low-batch traffic.
  6. Scale out: replicas with cache-aware routing; disaggregate prefill and decode only when measurements justify the complexity.
  7. Operate: autoscale on queue depth and cache usage, not CPU; set SLO-based alerts.

A decision table.

Goal Technique Improves Costs
Lower TTFT prefix caching, chunked prefill, smaller prompt TTFT cache memory
Lower TPOT speculative decoding, smaller or quantized model, less load TPOT draft memory, complexity
More requests per GPU continuous batching, KV quantization, GQA throughput tail latency if over-batched
Longer context cache offload, quantized cache, sliding window capacity transfer latency, quality risk

Everyday analogy. Speeding up a delivery company: measure where time goes (packing, driving, last mile), then fix the biggest block, rather than buying faster trucks for everything.

Common interview traps.

  • Jumping to "buy a bigger GPU" or "use a smaller model" before measuring where time goes.
  • Presenting speculation or quantization as free. Each has a cost and a regime where it loses.
  • Not knowing the units: be ready to give bytes per token, ms per token, and tokens per second with the arithmetic.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Generation is an autoregressive loop: one token per forward pass, each depending on all earlier tokens.
  • The KV cache stores the key and value tensors of past tokens per layer and KV head, so each step computes only the newest token. It trades memory for compute: bytes per token = 2 x layers x kv_heads x head_dim x bytes per value (128 KiB per token for a Llama-3-8B-style model in fp16, so about 1 GiB at 8k tokens).
  • Cache memory, not compute, usually caps the batch size. GQA/MQA/MLA, KV quantization, sliding windows and offloading shrink it; PagedAttention removes fragmentation using fixed-size blocks and block tables; prefix caching reuses identical token prefixes.
  • Prefill processes the whole prompt in parallel and is compute-bound; decode emits one token per step and is memory-bandwidth-bound (about 1 FLOP per byte at batch 1), which is why batching and speculation help.
  • TTFT (queue + prefill) and TPOT (decode speed) are separate; E2E = TTFT + TPOT x (N - 1). Report p95/p99, and use goodput against an SLO, not raw tokens per second.
  • Continuous batching schedules at every decode step, freeing slots and admitting requests immediately; it beats static batching several-fold on mixed workloads. Chunked prefill prevents long prompts from stalling streams.
  • Speculative decoding: a cheap draft proposes gamma tokens, the target verifies them in one pass; output is lossless. Expected tokens per pass = (1 - alpha^(gamma+1)) / (1 - alpha); gains vanish if the draft is costly, acceptance is low or the batch is large.
  • In production, watch queue length, cache usage, prefix hit rate, preemptions and tail latency; cancel abandoned requests; keep stable content at the front of prompts; and measure before optimising.
